title: Saga pattern
description: Learn the saga pattern for managing distributed transactions. Understand choreography and coordination approaches for long-running transactions.

data.text: The saga pattern manages distributed transactions by breaking them into a sequence of local transactions, each with compensating actions to undo changes if the saga fails. This provides eventual consistency without the blocking problems of two-phase commit.
A saga is a sequence of transactions where each transaction updates data within a single service. If any step fails, compensating transactions undo the effects of previous steps.

items: Break distributed transaction into local transactions
Each step is a normal ACID transaction within one service
Compensating actions undo previous steps on failure
Eventually consistent—temporary inconsistency during execution
Non-blocking—no long-held locks across services

data.title: Key Benefit
data.text: Sagas avoid the blocking and availability problems of 2PC while still providing a way to coordinate distributed operations.

items.title: Choreography
items.description: Services emit events and react to events from other services. Decentralized, no central coordinator. Can become complex with many services.

items.title: Orchestration
items.description: Central coordinator service manages the saga. Centralized logic, easier to understand. Coordinator becomes a single point of complexity.

data.text: In choreography, each service emits events and listens for events from other services.

items: Service A completes its transaction and emits an event
Service B listens for the event and executes its transaction
Service B emits an event for the next step
If a step fails, the service emits a compensating event
Previous services listen for compensating events and undo

data.title: When to Use
data.text: Simple sagas with few services, when you want decentralization, when you're already using an event-driven architecture.
In orchestration, a central coordinator service manages the entire saga.

items: Coordinator defines the saga workflow
Coordinator tells each service when to execute
Coordinator tracks saga state and progress
On failure, coordinator executes compensating actions
Single place to understand the business logic

data.title: When to Use
data.text: Complex sagas with many steps, when you need central visibility, when you want simpler business logic in individual services.
Compensating actions undo the effects of a transaction. They must be idempotent and always succeed.

items: Must be idempotent—may be called multiple times
Should be simple and reliable
Don't need to restore exact previous state
Just need to bring system to consistent state
Design them as part of the transaction design

data.title: Not Always Possible
data.text: Some operations can't be compensated (e.g., sending an email). Design your system to minimize these or accept the consequences.

items: Keep sagas short—minimize the window of inconsistency
Design compensating actions as first-class operations
Monitor saga execution and failures
Implement saga state persistence for recovery
Consider idempotency for all saga steps
Document the saga workflow clearly
Pros: Avoids blocking, better availability, scalable
Cons: Temporary inconsistency, complex to implement
Choreography: Decentralized but hard to reason about
Orchestration: Centralized but adds coordination service
